To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the density of social networks is proportional to the density of the population and the distance between them, 2) in the case of a disaster, the density is also proportional to the distance between the disaster epicenter and the population.

(a) the distribution of friends on a social network can be modeled by a simple function of population density, geographic distance and the number of friends per person, (b) information propagation can be modeled as a function of the number of friends of each node, (c) the number of friends can be estimated by a function of the geographic distance, population density and the number of ‘friends per capita’.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a model for predicting the extent of disaster effects based on the monitoring and analysis of social network traffic.
the following questions: (i) what are the models of SN friends distribution?
the development of models for the analysis of social network traffic and the prediction of the consequences of disasters based on the monitoring social network traffic.

the proposed models of SN friends distribution and information propagation can be used for the prediction of the spread of the information and the extent of the damage caused by the disaster.

it is a model of the SN traffic in disaster situations, which is based on the SN traffic in normal situations.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the social network traffic features in the disaster situation are not random, but are governed by a specific model, and that the monitoring of these features allows the estimation of the disaster gravity.
the SN traffic in disaster situations can be modeled and used to predict the extent of damage and the number of casualties.

the social network traffic in a disaster situation is characterized by the following features: (1) it is highly concentrated in time, (2) it is highly localized in space, and (3) it exhibits an exponential decay of the traffic volume with respect to the distance from the disaster epicenter.
